title: How ThePrimeagen got past "do I still have value?": good engineering decisions compound
summary: ThePrimeagen describes a six-month funk asking whether 20 years of Vim, languages and generalist skills still matter in the AI era. His answer: taste and line counts are not the value; accumulated engineering decision-making is, and the cost of the right line of code rises as code gets cheap.

principles.text: When code gets cheap to generate, the right line of code becomes more valuable, not less.
principles.quote: if the cost of a line of code has dramatically dropped, then the cost of the right line of code has dramatically increased.

principles.text: Engineering decisions compound; AI as a multiplier only works if you make good ones, or you end up forking Chromium.
principles.quote: if AI is to be a true multiplier, then every one of those little decisions actually do matter. Because if you don't, you're forking Chromium.

principles.text: Your value is real engineering decision-making (data formats, serialization, schemas), not taste and not lines of code.
principles.quote: I don't mean taste, I mean actual engineering decision-making that goes into this.

principles.text: With unlimited options, picking the right one gets harder; experience is what lets you choose well.
principles.quote: when you have every option, it actually becomes dramatically harder to pick the right option.

principles.text: Don't chase constant visible output. Earning experience beats instant completion, and failing to understand why teaches the most.
principles.quote: earning experience is more valuable than completing something instantaneously.

principles.text: Spending hours debugging instead of reading the manual is a legitimate way to learn.
principles.quote: I decided to save 5 minutes of reading the friendly manual with 6 hours of debugging, and I learned a lot from that.
